function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a CI job) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repository.

> **NOTE** – The helper functions you provided only generate Dockerfiles for Python images, so I’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile for a Node.js app.  
> The Kubernetes YAML is generated via the `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` function, and the GitHub Actions workflow is written manually.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use HTTPS instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) and a `package.json`.  
A minimal Dockerfile for this setup looks like:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

We’ll generate a Deployment + Service that exposes the app on port **3000**.  
Using the helper function:

```python
# In a Python REPL or a small script
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="my-node-app:latest",  # replace with your registry/tag
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

> The function will create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or you can rename it to `deployment.yaml`).  
> If you prefer to write it manually, here’s the equivalent YAML:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: my-node-app:latest   # <-- update with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
        with:
          manifests: k8s.yaml
          images: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` secrets to the repo.  
> * If you want automatic deployment, add a `KUBECONFIG` secret pointing to your cluster.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Dockerfile** in the repo root.
* A **k8s.yaml** (or `deployment.yaml`) file with the Deployment & Service.
* A **.github/workflows/ci.yml** that builds the image on every push to `main`.

The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build and push the Docker image whenever you push to `main`. If you added the optional deployment step, it will also apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster.

That’s it! 🎉
